### Intel signs first external customer for advanced 18A chips
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/6c300267f1652815
- Primary Source: CNBC (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/intel-first-18a-foundry-customer.html)
- Executive Summary: Intel's CEO announced at the TomorrowX Summit that the company has signed its first external customer for the 18A process node, which entered risk production in June. This milestone aims to validate Intel's foundry turnaround strategy and alleviate capacity constraints for hyperscalers currently over-reliant on TSMC.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Intel CEO; Pushkar Ranade, Intel's technology chief (TomorrowX Summit, Austin, Texas): Signed first external customer for 18A process node; process is in risk production
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To validate foundry turnaround strategy and reduce reliance on TSMC-only supply chains
* [Key Metrics] government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, as optimism grew around the prospect of U.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] The order is vital for financial recovery amidst declining PC sales and capacity supply chain challenges.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on Wednesday that the company has signed the first outside customer for its 18A chips.
> "Resilient supply on the foundry is very important,"Tan said at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas. "And then 18A, I'm involved in production and we just signed the first customer,"Tan added, without naming the debut client.
> It's a milestone moment for Intel in its five-year effort to take on chip manufacturing leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. After years of missteps and low yields, Intel touted 18A as key to a turnaround that would finally convert the company into a competitive chip manufacturer for non-Intel products.
> "It's a huge win for foundry,"Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin told CNBC in an interview.
> Pushkar Ranade, Intel's technology chief, clarified on X that the external customer had signed up for Intel's 18A-P manufacturing process node, which went into risk production in June. In May, reports indicated that Apple and Intel were closing in on a deal to use Intel's foundry to make some of the chips for Apple devices.
> Intel's stock has lost more than half its value since the end of September, with most of that plunge coming late last month after the company said revenue this quarter will be at least $1 billion shy of analysts' estimates due to a PC sales slump and supply chain challenges.
> In considering who the customer may be, Bajarin pointed to Nvidia, Apple or the major hyperscalers that make their own custom processors.
> "Amazon, Microsoft and Google are struggling to get capacity for their CPU ambitions at TSMC,"he said. "So it makes sense that you go somewhere for at least some capacity."
> Tan said in late October that he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion, but that Intel can't currently meet customer demand.
> Wall Street has turned on Intel of late after the chipmaker had become a top trade starting in the middle of last year. The U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, as optimism grew around the prospect of U.S.-made chips that could replace an almost complete reliance on Taiwan.
> Until now, Intel has had no marquee customer for its foundry business, primarily manufacturing chips for its own products at its factories, including a huge new campus in Arizona.
> Intel is a leader in another step of the chipmaking process known as advanced packaging, where individual chips are packaged together and connected to the larger system. Tan also announced on Wednesday that Microsoft is its first publicly named customer for its most advanced packaging technology, known as EMIB.
> — CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

### How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/7b058802ee207ea6
- Primary Source: New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/nvidia-alibaba-china-military.html?unlocked_article_code=1.RlE.LNs4.VaGPGt5WhYLb&smid=url-share)
- Executive Summary: Nvidia chips were routed through the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed to Alibaba-related entities, which maintain ties with the Zhejiang Lab, raising U.S. concerns over high-end chip access for military-linked AI research. Despite personal connections, the multi-layered supply chain and obfuscation tactics have significantly complicated regulatory compliance.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Nvidia, Megaspeed, Alibaba, Zhejiang Lab: Utilizing intermediaries for chip procurement linked to military-affiliated AI research
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] To circumvent U.S. trade restrictions and acquire high-performance computing for tactical AI applications
* [Key Fact Detail] Nvidia chips funneled to military-affiliated labs through intermediaries.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Nvidia faces heightened compliance pressure and stricter supply chain audits.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.
> Working from a colonial mansion in the city’s former French Concession neighborhood, the couple boasted about Ms. Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, who they said would guarantee a supply of powerful computer chips.
> They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.
> Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.
> For the past several weeks, Nvidia has been convulsed by revelations that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.
> The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.
> The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.
> Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.
> The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.
> Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.
> The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.
> In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.
> In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. Mr. Huang resigned last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.
> Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military issued hundreds of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.
> “Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.
> James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.
> Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.
> “Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.
> A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”
> Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.
> During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.
> Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.
> “He is the hero. He’s an incredible hero. A superhero,” Mr. Huang said to Mr. Wang onstage, noting his work with young people. It is not clear if he knew of the lab’s military ties.
> Mr. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Wang stretched back more than a decade. After Mr. Wang built Alibaba’s cloud unit, it became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying chips for a cloud service that was used by businesses and government.
> The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.
> But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.
> Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.
> At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.
> A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.
> Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.
> A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.
> Some of the work done by researchers at the lab has run on Nvidia chips, which are more powerful and more popular than those of Chinese rivals. Nvidia researchers even copublished studies with authors from Zhejiang Lab.
> Alibaba also won contracts for three stages of a computing center that provincial officials describe as built by the lab. The contracts were issued by a state-owned company, Zhejiang Computility, that sells computing power to the lab. Zhejiang Computility advertises access to export-controlled Nvidia chips. The technical specifications in a separate contract it signed with another supplier match those of Nvidia chips.
> Mr. Wang has said insufficient access to A.I. computing power has held China back.
> “If China is to walk at the forefront of artificial intelligence,” he said, “we still lack high-quality computing power.”
> But when Zhejiang Computility sought bids for the computing cluster in 2024, Nvidia was barred from selling chips that powerful to China. Another supplier to the company that year, Hangjin Technology, has a joint venture with Century Litong, another company linked to Mr. Kang and Ms. Huang, the former Megaspeed executive.
> In September 2025, a few months after Mr. Huang’s visit with Mr. Wang, Nvidia and Alibaba announced a new collaboration: Nvidia’s robotic development tools would be integrated into Alibaba’s cloud to help train autonomous vehicles and robots.
> In December 2023, Jensen Huang’s company plane made an overnight stop in Malaysia during a tour of Asia to meet with the country’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim. Announcing a deal for a data center in the country’s southern state of Johor, Mr. Huang said Malaysia had the potential to become an A.I. “manufacturing” hub for the world.
> The project, on a former palm plantation larger than Central Park, was to be built by the Malaysian industrial conglomerate YTL. Nvidia pledged to provide some of its most advanced chips.
> The setup was part of a multibillion-dollar data center boom underway in Malaysia that has made it one of the world’s largest computing hubs. Across the southern state of Johor, cranes swirl over massive construction projects underway to meet the demand from Chinese and American companies.
> It is here that these webs of companies from China, Singapore and elsewhere form the opaque supply chains.
> At the YTL facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated Nvidia chips inside the facility on behalf of Alibaba, according to five people familiar with the project who were not authorized to speak publicly.
> Computer systems running on YTL’s network at the facility also bear Alibaba’s name, according to an infrastructure analysis by Infrawatch, an intelligence firm. That included software to remotely monitor equipment at a data center.
> YTL did not respond to requests for comment.
> The arrangement shows how Alibaba used a network of companies in Malaysia and other Southeast Asian countries to access powerful Nvidia chips that they would not otherwise be able to purchase or bring to China.
> Alibaba’s links to the YTL facility in Malaysia help explain how the process worked, according to two people familiar with the development.
> First, Alibaba would pledge to be a customer of a regional company, like Megaspeed. Then Megaspeed would use that agreement to raise money from investors to buy Nvidia chips, said the people. After securing the chips, Megaspeed struck more deals with companies like YTL that built data centers to operate the chips. Sometimes, the people said, chips bound for the data center were smuggled into China.
> Once the facilities were up and running in recent years, Alibaba and its customers could access the Nvidia chips remotely. From the Malaysian data center, fiber optic cables send data to an internet connection hub in Singapore, which then links to China through undersea cables.
> American officials believe China’s military uses the overseas data centers to train A.I. models, but then runs its A.I. operations from facilities inside China.
> Nvidia’s Mr. Huang argued that China’s government would never accept the security risks of using foreign data centers and chips. But China-linked companies are involved at each step of the process.
> Megaspeed buys its Nvidia servers from a company called Aivres, which is an American subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech giant with deep state ties. At Megaspeed's new data center, repairs and installation are also done by engineers from another Shanghai company, connected to Ms. Huang, according to two people familiar with the operations.
> Other Chinese tech giants have created similar arrangements to access Nvidia chips. In Southeast Asia, data center companies including DayOne, Bridge Data Centers and Aolani provide computing power to customers based in China, according to public records and people familiar with the deals.
> DayOne and Bridge Data Centers did not respond to requests for comment. Aolani declined to comment about its customers.
> Now the future of the boom has been thrown into question. American officials recently strengthened export rules to prevent companies like Alibaba from remotely accessing Nvidia’s chips.
> That puts projects like the YTL facility in Malaysia in the spotlight. YTL’s stock price fell about 20 percent over two weeks as scrutiny grew of Megaspeed’s operations in the country.
> If things go bad for Megaspeed, Alibaba put a contingency in place. A business agreement between an Alibaba subsidiary and Megaspeed pledges all servers, chips, intellectual property, and other equipment back to Alibaba if Megaspeed fails to meet its contractual obligations.

### US Charges Russian as Foreign Agent Targeting Palantir Workers
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/62f224a44fbd70bd
- Primary Source: Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-18/us-charges-russian-as-foreign-agent-targeting-palantir-workers)
- Executive Summary: The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia. On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents. According
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Industry Leaders: US Charges Russian as Foreign Agent Targeting Palantir Workers
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.
* [Key Technical Spec] US Charges Russian as Foreign Agent Targeting Palantir Workers.
* [Industry Analysis] On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.
> On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.
> According to officials, D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully this summer after being recruited by co-conspirators through Telegram. His alleged mission was to “carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California”, the justice department said, without identifying the company or the alleged co-conspirators.
> Bloomberg reported that the company in question was Palantir Technologies, citing an unnamed source familiar with the matter. The firm has a large office in Palo Alto.
> The department added that D’iu had reportedly received instructions, equipment and financial support from the co-conspirators, who told him that his work was for “the Motherland”.
> They also allegedly instructed him to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.
> The Russian embassy was contacted for comment.
> In June, D’iu allegedly traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the US-Mexico border. After entering the US, he was allegedly instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software to “facilitate his assignments”.
> View image in fullscreen Igor D’iu’s allegedly falsified US passport. Photograph: US Department of JusticeD’iu’s co-conspirators also allegedly directed him to visit a cafe near the company’s Palo Alto office, identify employees and photograph their laptop screens as they worked. They further instructed him to “position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity”, the justice department said.
> The alleged surveillance gradually expanded, with D’iu allegedly instructed to monitor employees and their residences. The justice department said he reportedly conducted online searches for multiple employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive.
> In early September, D’iu allegedly followed a female employee in a silver Lexus SUV for nearly 30 miles (48km) as she drove from the company’s Palo Alto office toward San Francisco. According to the justice department, the employee repeatedly attempted to evade him, at one point driving into a grocery store parking lot.
> Officials said D’iu “allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle”. The employee eventually called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco police department’s Mission station.
> D’iu allegedly abandoned the pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. The justice department added that investigators had also obtained evidence indicating he had followed other employees on previous occasions.
> View image in fullscreen Igor D’iu’s Russian passport. Photograph: US Department of JusticeAfter Palo Alto police contacted D’iu about the alleged stalking incident, he reportedly changed vehicles and obtained a new phone number. His co-conspirators then allegedly instructed him to travel to Reno, Nevada, before he returned to the Bay Area to continue his assignments, the justice department said.
> The justice department also accused D’iu of obtaining fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity. Investigators reportedly intercepted two international packages containing concealed ID documents, including a fake California ID card and an altered US passport. Officials said the passport was authentic and had originally been issued to another individual in the US before being modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.
> Investigators also discovered a social security card bearing the name “Hugo Landry Johns”. During an FBI search of D’iu’s East Palo Alto residence in October, investigators recovered approximately $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment and additional fraudulent ID documents.
> They also found a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, several of which belonged to the residences of company employees. The notebook also included detailed profiles of at least three employees, documenting their family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and an “assessment of their strengths and weaknesses”.
> In response to the indictment, M Scott Proctor, acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, said: “The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies.
> “As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of US sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation,” he added.

### U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/f79c05a76000c517
- Primary Source: New York Times (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/google-gemini-ai-search-schools-nyc-la-chicago.html?unlocked_article_code=1.RVE.gLxg.XpnU5fMGh-0k&smid=url-share)
- Executive Summary: Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said. Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Natasha Singer and Dana Goldstein: U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
* [Context & Motivation] school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.
* [Key Fact Detail] U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
* [Industry Analysis] But there will be no version of search available.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Three of the largest U.S. school districts, New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago, are considering using alternate search engines after Google this month refused to remove artificial intelligence from search tools used by students, officials said.
> Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A.I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A.I. will lose access to an important learning tool.
> Google’s approach created a firestorm of criticism from lawmakers, government officials, education leaders and parents, some of whom said the tech giant was trying to force its A.I. into public schools.
> Now, some schools across the United States are blocking Google’s A.I. in search — or considering alternative providers.
> “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options,” Kamar H. Samuels, the chancellor of New York City schools, said in a statement. “We refuse to accept the false binary Google has laid out.”
> Google’s new use-it-or-lose-it stance on A.I. in search underscores how the tech giant’s interlocking ecosystem of Chromebook laptops and apps like Gmail and Docs has become essential classroom infrastructure. The company’s search engine is a go-to product for teaching students how to do research and find primary sources.
> But some educators worry that the generative A.I. that Google has embedded in its search engine for consumers could hinder students’ critical thinking, undermine learning and present safety risks. Some students have used the chatbots embedded in search to cheat, they have said, or scanned A.I.-generated search summaries instead of reading historical documents and news sources.
> Educators are balancing those concerns with the reality that A.I. has already become an important tool in the work force, that a majority of U.S. teenagers already use chatbots and that many students will need to use A.I. in their future jobs.
> Medical associations have also warned that developing relationships with chatbots could have negative mental health effects on young people. Earlier this month, two parents in North Carolina sued Google, saying their daughter had developed a plan to die by suicide after prolonged chats with the company’s A.I. on search on her school Chromebook. (Google said it had built safeguards into its A.I. features in search to help young people find emergency resources and was reviewing the claims in the lawsuit.)
> Now districts like Chicago Public Schools, the fourth-largest U.S. school system, are urging Google to provide them with a version of search without A.I. features. “If such an arrangement can’t be reached,” Chicago Public Schools said in an email, “the district will look to other search solutions.”
> Among the search engine alternatives for schools: DuckDuckGo and Microsoft’s Bing. Both offer options to disable A.I.-generated answers.
> Google argued this month that it would be providing schools with more options to control student A.I. access — not fewer. Administrators could give students access to A.I. Mode, a chatbot-like function in search, as well as A.I. Overview, which summarizes search results, the company said. It is also pilot testing Guided Learning, a new chatbot widget intended to break down academic questions for students without providing easy answers.
> “We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” Google said in a statement, noting that next year the company would turn off its Gemini app and search engine for schools “until schools decide which services to enable.”
> Over the last three years, the company has made building generative A.I. a top business priority. And Google has integrated its Gemini A.I. chatbot throughout its software suite.
> The fight over Google’s A.I. products has been brewing for months, with district leaders and teachers across the country approaching Google employees at meetings and online to request greater control over how students interact with generative A.I.
> School tech directors in four states said they and their colleagues had repeatedly pressed Google this year to let schools decide which A.I. tools, if any, might be appropriate for students in different grades. And they warned that Google’s all-or-nothing approach to search essentially overrode more nuanced school policies on student A.I. use.
> “We need to be able to control our own pace,” said Chris Warden, the technology director at Central R-3 School District in Park Hills, Mo., “not have Google tell us what the pace of A.I. adoption is going to be.”
> In September, the New York City Department of Education and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced moratoriums on student use of generative A.I.
> At the start of this school year, Google’s education team helped Los Angeles schools turn off A.I. mode for students logged into their school Google accounts, according to school board members. But Google said during its announcement this month that its A.I. features were so “deeply integrated” in search that it could not provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine.
> Google’s decision prompted groups of parents to protest last week in front of the company’s Boston, Boulder, Chicago, New York and Portland offices.
> In Chicago, several dozen parents and educators chanted slogans like, “Hey, Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini.”
> “We don’t want corporations determining what is happening in our kids’ classrooms and how our schools are run,” said Cassie Creswell, the executive director of a parent group called Illinois Families for Public Schools, who helped organize the Chicago rally.
> Parents and students also protested in Venice, Calif., carrying signs like “We don’t need Alphabet to teach the alphabet.”
> At a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee two days later, Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, was applauded when he said, “We have choices” as to which company’s software to use. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight,” he added.
> This week, Jenn Brown, a Google program manager, offered an explanation for the company’s refusal to provide schools with a chatbot-free search engine for students. Google now considers search to be fundamentally an A.I. product, she said during a monthly Google Meet for school tech leaders, according to a school administrator who attended the discussion.
> New York City, Los Angeles and other school districts said they were using a combination of software controls and filters to independently block student access to A.I. in Google search. Even so, some New York City parents have found students can still easily access A.I. Mode at home when signed into their student Google accounts.
> New York City has declined to participate in the pilot of Google’s new chatbot feature for students, according to the district. Instead, the district is conducting its own research of five other A.I. tools for potential use at the high-school level.
> In the absence of A.I. controls from Google, some smaller school districts are also working to independently disable chatbots in search. In Missouri, Mr. Warden said his rural school district, which serves about 2,000 students, had signed up for a new service from Lightspeed Systems, an online student monitoring service for schools. The software is designed to block student access to A.I. Overview and A.I. Mode in Google search.
> The backlash against Google has complicated some school districts’ plans to teach students how to use chatbots effectively, said Nick Melvoin, a Los Angeles school board member.
> “Ironically, it undermines the goal of trying to get some A.I. into schools,” Mr. Melvoin said.

### Palo Alto raises annual forecast, signs $4.5 billion deal for Applied Compute
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/bbaed9f2dc4a466d
- Primary Source: Reuters (https://www.reuters.com/technology/palo-alto-buy-ai-startup-applied-compute-45-billion-2026-11-18/)
- Executive Summary: Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks is acquiring AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion and has raised its FY2027 revenue guidance. The acquisition seeks to integrate AI infrastructure management with cybersecurity, mitigating risks associated with open-weight model deployment.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Palo Alto Networks (CEO Nikesh Arora): Acquired Applied Compute for $4.5B; raised FY revenue guidance
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Mitigating security risks in enterprise AI model deployment
* [Key Metrics] $4.5 billion strategic acquisition of Applied Compute.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Establishing a defensive framework for AI infrastructure.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> A Palo Alto Networks logo is seen in this illustration taken August 18, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration
> Nov 18 : Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and signed a deal to acquire AI startup Applied Compute in a deal valued at $4.5 billion, as a heightened threat environment pushes customers toward broader security products.
> Shares of Palo Alto jumped about 10 per cent in after-hours trading to $368.60, and drove gains in rivals. CrowdStrike rose 5.3 per cent, Zscaler climbed 3 per cent and Fortinet gained 2.1 per cent.
> Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi.
> The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks, giving attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.
> "As AI accelerates cyber attacks, enterprises are moving with urgency to replace disjointed tools with unified platforms," Palo Alto CEO Nikesh Arora said during the company's analyst call on Wednesday.
> With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto is looking to offer users a technology platform to help customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.
> Open-weight models, AI systems whose trained settings are publicly released, present security challenges, including the risk of model tampering, data leakage and misuse by bad actors.
> "Applied Compute extends Palo Alto's push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI. The opportunity is to bring AI infrastructure and security closer together," said Shaul Eyal, analyst at TD Cowen.
> The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
> Palo Alto now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its prior expectation of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion.
> Its first-quarter revenue came in at $3.45 billion, up 39 per cent from a year earlier, beating estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.

- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Terrence O'Brien: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
* [Context & Motivation] New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times.
* [Key Fact Detail] Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search.

> New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”
> Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”
> In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”
> Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

### Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/fff52c1181f216dc
- Primary Source: Wired AI (https://www.wired.com/story/guys-really-we-got-this/)
- Executive Summary: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s mo
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Lauren Goode: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.
* [Key Fact Detail] Nvidia is going through it.
* [Industry Analysis] So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s mo.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era.
> Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce. And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.”
> By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it:
> Tuesday’s earnings call:
> “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.”
> Wednesday’s all-hands meeting:
> “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.”
> Wednesday’s all-hands meeting, again:
> Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together.
> “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.”
> Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?)
> Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment.
> Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase, adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post.
> And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot.
> Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.
> Paresh Dave contributed to this article.
